claims.text: High-temperature degradation of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by competitive, synergistic oxidation of its reactive elements.
Under oxidizing atmospheres, Cr and Ti oxidize rapidly and preferentially.
Preferential Cr and Ti oxidation produces discontinuous, multilayer oxide scales.
Cr- and Ti-rich oxide formation impedes development of a protective Al2O3 barrier.
The discontinuous multilayer scales undergo spallation and cause mechanical embrittlement.
A reducing atmosphere suppresses extensive external scale formation because of its lower oxidative drive.
Reducing exposure promotes internal oxidation along grain boundaries.
The balance between external and internal oxidation is determined by competing oxide-formation kinetics among the alloying elements.
Cr and Ti diffuse to the surface during oxidizing exposure.
Al2O3 develops more slowly than the competing Cr- and Ti-bearing oxides but would be protective if continuous.
The as-built additively manufactured alloy has a homogeneous fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy is free of large-scale oxide formations.
Before elevated-temperature exposure, the alloy has high strength and fatigue resistance.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a thick, defective, multilayer scale with discontinuity and spallation relative to the starting-state baseline and reducing exposure.
The oxidizing-exposure scale will cause marked surface embrittlement and mechanical degradation.
Reducing exposure will produce measurable grain-boundary internal oxidation and localized embrittlement despite limited external oxidation.
The proposed comparison uses identical thermal histories and sample geometries while varying the atmosphere between air containing 21% O2 and 5% H2 in N2.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply from 800 to 1000 degrees Celsius for exposures of 50 to 200 hours under the specified gas compositions.
Variations in elemental segregation or scale adhesion may alter the degradation rate.
